citation: Charoenpit, Saromporn, and Michiko Ohkura. "Exploring Emotion in an E-learning System Using Eye Tracking." International Journal of Affective Engineering 14, no. 4 (2015): 309-316. https://doi.org/10.5057/ijae.IJAE-D-14-29.
discipline: affective engineering / e-learning HCI, correlating eye-tracking metrics with self-reported learner emotion in a prototype e-learning system
thesis: Charoenpit and Ohkura address a stated gap -- 'to date, few e-learning systems have derived emotions from eye tracking data' -- by building on their own earlier biological-signal-focused e-learning system to design and test a prototype that records learners' eye movements while they study two units of introductory C-programming content. They ask whether eye-metric indexes (fixation counts, fixation durations, and pupil diameter, each computed inside versus outside a defined Learning Area) track two 'emotion groups' constructed from a nine-item post-content questionnaire: an interest group and a boredom group. The paper's own contribution claim, restated in the Conclusion, is narrower than the introduction's framing suggests: of the several eye-metric indexes tested, only the fixation-number ratio and the fixation-duration ratio are put forward as 'useful,' while the pupil-diameter ratio's relationship to the two emotion groups is reported but sits in tension with the interpretive rule the authors themselves state for it (a high pupil-diameter ratio is said to indicate boredom, yet the ratio correlates positively with interest and negatively with boredom in the reported tables).

sections.title: Abstract/keywords
sections.summary: States the gap (few e-learning systems derive emotion from eye tracking data), previews the prototype, names the two target emotion groups (interest, boredom).

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates eye tracking as an interest/attention indicator, citing Duchowski's Eye Tracking Methodology [5]; restates the gap and the paper's aim.

sections.title: 2. Literature review
sections.summary: Five cited eye-tracking-in-e-learning studies: Hend & Remya on indirect attention/stress/fatigue measures [6]; a study named in-text 'Ismail and Mohamed' but numbered as Haddioui & Khaldi [7] (an in-text/reference-list name mismatch reproduced as found); Al-Wabil et al. ('Areej et al.') on eye gaze and learning-style scales [8]; Porta, Ricotti & Perez ('Marco et al.') on gaze coordinates, fixation duration, pupil diameter, and blink rate during problem-solving [9]; Mealha et al. on eye-tracking visualization techniques across domains [10].

sections.title: 3. Design of e-learning system
sections.summary: The authors' prior five-module architecture [11]: learners, instructors, web/database/LMS servers, biological sensors (ECG, EEG, eye tracking), and an 'analysis of learner emotions' module naming three emotion models -- Russell's Circumplex [12], a model the text labels 'Shen' [13], and 'Kort's learning spiral' [14] -- though the numbered reference list itself associates [13] with Kort, Reilly & Picard (2001) and [14] with Kaiser & Oertel (2006), a second apparent citation-numbering inconsistency reproduced as found.

sections.title: 4. Experiment -- 4.1 Method
sections.summary: Two counterbalanced content/style patterns (Table 1: Content 1 = C-programming loops, Content 2 = decision-making statements, described as more difficult; Style A = text-only, Style B = text+pictures); 11-step procedure (calibration, pre/post-tests, 5-minute break, two questionnaires); nine-item 5-point Likert questionnaire (Table 2, interest group 6 items / boredom group 3 items, sourced from [15,16]); EyeTech Quick Glance v5.0 apparatus, 50 Hz.

sections.title: 4.2 Experimental results and discussion
sections.summary: Table 3 (test scores + questionnaire means); Table 4 (eye metrics -- fixation count, fixation duration, pupil diameter -- in Learning Area (LA) vs. Out-of-Learning-Area (OLA), Figure 5, plus derived LA/OLA ratios); Tables 5-6 (correlation coefficients with interest/boredom group means, Figures 6-7); the User 04 self-report/eye-metric mismatch case study; Table 7 (independent-samples t-test, Content 1 vs. 2, Figures 8-9).

sections.title: 5. Conclusion
sections.summary: Names the fixation-number ratio and fixation-duration ratio as the useful eye-metric indexes identified; states future work toward a new experiment to help learners manage negative emotions (boredom) and sustain attention/motivation.

sections.title: Acknowledgments, references, author bios
sections.summary: Shibaura Institute of Technology funding; eight Brazilian volunteer participants thanked; 19 references; author biographies (Charoenpit, Ohkura).

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: treated only operationally, never named as such: 'boredom' is the mean of three within-session questionnaire items (Table 2) answered once per content unit, implicitly state/situational; no trait instrument (e.g., a Boredom Proneness Scale) administered or discussed

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: the paper's operational core; the Learning Area (LA) vs. Out-of-Learning-Area (OLA) screen partition (Figure 5) operationalizes attention as fixation location, following the claim that eye data 'indicate a person's interest level and the focus of her attention' (citing Hend & Remya [6]); disengagement is read off as elevated OLA fixation counts/durations relative to LA

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: the 'interest' group is this paper's engagement pole, built from six of the nine questionnaire items and grounded in the same three-model apparatus (Russell's Circumplex, 'Shen,' 'Kort's learning spiral') used to define both emotion groups

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: not treated; no trait instrument administered or discussed

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: not named; the closest functional analog (gaze drifting into OLA) is read purely as attentional disengagement, not as directed or contentful thought

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: not independently theorized beyond the boredom-group questionnaire items themselves ('tiring,' 'anxiety-inducing,' 'frustrating' -- Table 2, items 4/5/8)

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: not treated; subjective time is never discussed

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: not treated; boredom is framed purely instrumentally, a negative state to detect and eventually help learners 'deal with,' not an adaptive or regulatory signal

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom, being-bored-by, being-bored-with (FCM forms)
constructs.treatment: not treated; no phenomenological vocabulary or Heideggerian literature present anywhere in the source

measures.label: pupil dilation / pupillometry
measures.signal: pupil diameter (mm), recorded separately in Learning Area (LA) and Out-of-Learning-Area (OLA); derived pupil-diameter ratio (LA/OLA)
measures.apparatus: EyeTech Quick Glance hardware v5.0, 50 Hz sampling
measures.keyResult: stated interpretive rule: 'high pupil diameter ratio indicates that learner is bored,' but the ratio correlates positively with interest in Content 1 (r=.694**) and Style A (r=.665**), and negatively with boredom in Content 2 (r=-.790*) and Style B (r=-.826*) -- an internally inconsistent measure-to-construct mapping the source does not flag

measures.label: gaze variance / fixation dispersion
measures.signal: number of fixations and fixation duration (s), recorded separately in LA and OLA; derived fixation-number ratio and fixation-duration ratio (LA/OLA)
measures.apparatus: EyeTech Quick Glance hardware v5.0, 50 Hz sampling; two-area-of-interest (LA/OLA) screen partition (Figure 5)
measures.keyResult: fixation-duration ratio in Content 1 (r=.831**) and fixation-number ratio in Content 1 (r=.673*) correlate positively with interest; fixation-duration ratio (r=-.656**) and fixation-number ratio (r=-.690**) in Content 2 correlate negatively with boredom; OLA fixation count in Content 2 correlates negatively with interest (r=-.778*); Conclusion names these two ratios as the paper's 'useful eye metric indexes'

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.signal: nine-item, 5-point Likert post-content questionnaire (Table 2), split into an interest group (6 items) and a boredom group (3 items: tiring/anxiety/frustrating); items selected from two external instruments
measures.apparatus: on-screen/paper questionnaire administered after each content unit's post-test
measures.keyResult: interest-group means generally higher than boredom-group means across users/conditions; User 04 shows a mismatch against eye-metric evidence (boredom-group mean higher in Content 1 than Content 2, opposite of the eye-tracking pattern), attributed by the authors to questionnaire-timing lag

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.signal: ten-question pre-test and post-test (one point/question) per content unit, testing C-programming comprehension
measures.apparatus: on-screen quiz administered before and after each content unit
measures.keyResult: post-test scores generally exceeded pre-test scores (learning occurred), with three named exceptions (users 03, 04, 08); used to confirm learning rather than as an emotion index per se

measures.label: EEG frontal alpha asymmetry / EEG alpha-theta power / EEG functional connectivity / EEG eyes-open vs. eyes-closed
measures.apparatus: EEG named only as one of the prior system's [11] 'biological sensors' module alongside ECG; never recorded or analyzed in this study
measures.keyResult: no own finding; background/planned-architecture mention only

measures.label: blink / eye-closure
measures.apparatus: appears only in the literature review as a metric used by cited studies (Hend & Remya [6]; Porta, Ricotti & Perez [9])
measures.keyResult: no own finding; background context only

measures.label: heart rate / HRV
measures.apparatus: ECG named only as a planned 'biological sensor' category in the prior system architecture [11]
measures.keyResult: no own finding; background/planned-architecture mention only

measures.label: predictive-processing model
measures.keyResult: no predictive-processing framework used anywhere in the source

measures.label: ML classification
measures.apparatus: n/a; the analysis is limited to Pearson correlation and independent-samples t-tests
measures.keyResult: no classifier or generative model of any kind is used

readings.claim: Post-test scores generally exceeded pre-test scores, with three users (03, 04, 08) as named exceptions; interest-group questionnaire means were generally higher than boredom-group means across users and conditions.

Fixation-duration ratio, fixation-number ratio, and pupil-diameter ratio correlate positively with the interest-group questionnaire mean in Content 1 (and pupil-diameter ratio also in Style A); OLA fixation count correlates negatively with interest in Content 2.
Fixation-duration ratio, fixation-number ratio, and pupil-diameter ratio correlate negatively with the boredom-group questionnaire mean in Content 2 (and pupil-diameter ratio also in Style B).

The pupil-diameter ratio's negative correlation with the boredom-group mean runs contrary to the paper's own stated interpretive rule that a high pupil-diameter ratio indicates the learner is bored, which would predict a positive correlation; the source does not flag or resolve this internal inconsistency.
readings.stance: qualifies (our observation, not the source's own)

readings.claim: User 04's questionnaire and eye-metric evidence diverge: the boredom-group mean was higher for Content 1 than Content 2, while fixation-plot evidence shows the OLA-directed gaze pattern the authors associate with boredom occurring in Content 2; the authors attribute the mismatch to questionnaire-timing lag and conclude the eye-metric evidence is more precise/real-time than self-report.
An independent-samples t-test for User 04 found significant differences in OLA fixation number, duration, point, and length between Content 1 and Content 2, but no significant LA differences.

The Conclusion names the fixation-number ratio and fixation-duration ratio -- not the pupil-diameter ratio -- as the 'useful eye metric indexes' the experiment identified, and states future work toward an intervention experiment to help learners manage boredom and sustain attention/motivation.

concepts.term: number-of-fixation ratio / fixation-duration ratio / pupil-diameter ratio (LA/OLA)
interest group / boredom group (questionnaire-derived emotion groups)

tensions.axis: stated pupil-diameter-ratio interpretive rule ('high ratio = bored') vs. the sign of its own correlation results
tensions.note: the paper states that a high pupil-diameter ratio indicates the learner is bored, yet the ratio correlates positively with interest (Content 1, Style A) and negatively with boredom (Content 2, Style B) in its own tables -- the negative correlation with boredom is the opposite sign the stated rule would predict, and the source neither flags nor resolves the inconsistency.

tensions.axis: self-report (questionnaire) vs. eye-tracking evidence for a single participant (User 04)
tensions.note: questionnaire boredom-group means were higher in Content 1 than Content 2, while eye-metric/fixation-plot evidence points to boredom in Content 2; the authors resolve the conflict by trusting the eye-tracking channel, attributing the questionnaire result to administration lag, without independently validating this explanation.

tensions.axis: content difficulty vs. boredom as the driver of the observed eye-metric/questionnaire pattern
tensions.note: Content 2 (decision-making statements) is explicitly described as more difficult than Content 1 (loops), and is also the condition most consistently associated with boredom-correlated eye metrics; the source does not examine whether the observed pattern reflects difficulty/frustration rather than boredom proper.

tensions.axis: in-text citation names vs. numbered reference-list authors
tensions.note: two apparent internal inconsistencies reproduced as found: the literature-review citation named 'Ismail and Mohamed' [7] corresponds in the numbered reference list to Haddioui & Khaldi; and the three named emotion models ('Russell's circumplex' [12], 'Shen' [13], 'Kort's learning spiral' [14]) do not cleanly match the numbered references, where [13] is Kort, Reilly & Picard (2001) and [14] is Kaiser & Oertel (2006).

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- eye-tracking/emotion channel
dataset_channels.note: Charoenpit & Ohkura's Learning-Area/Out-of-Learning-Area (LA/OLA) area-of-interest partition, its three raw eye metrics (fixation count, fixation duration, pupil diameter) computed per area, and its derived LA/OLA ratios offer a concrete, low-cost precedent for classifying engagement versus boredom from eye-tracking data in an instructional setting. Unconfirmable until the dataset entry specifies its own apparatus and area-of-interest scheme; a VR headset's integrated eye tracker would track 3D gaze vectors against headset-relative regions rather than 2D screen coordinates against a fixed LA/OLA split, so translation is not immediate (P/anticipatory-application).
